nodes.ask: An abnormal electrolyte result, or symptoms that suggest one. First move?
options: ABC, cardiac monitor and a 12-lead ECG; blood gas for potassium
IV calcium gluconate for the reported potassium, before an ECG
Non-contrast CT head for the confusion first, then the ECG
A liter of 0.9% saline over an hour while the repeat bloods run
nodes.chainStep: ABC; cardiac monitor and a 12-lead ECG; blood gas potassium while the laboratory electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate and renal function run
nodes.why: The ECG shows what potassium, calcium and magnesium are doing to the heart: UKKA wants an urgent 12-lead for a potassium of 6.0 or more and continuous monitoring at 6.5 or with ECG features, and a blood gas analyser gives the potassium while the laboratory result is awaited. A high calcium shortens the QT and a low calcium prolongs it. Urine osmolality and sodium define the cause of hyponatremia after the emergency treatment, not before it, because severe symptoms need hypertonic saline whatever the cause. Saline before the electrolyte is known can harm: in SIADH isotonic saline may not correct the sodium and can worsen it.

nodes.summary: Arrest or shock: resuscitation first. When hyperkalemia is known or suspected, UKKA gives IV calcium chloride, 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose and sodium bicarbonate, and considers dialysis during CPR if it is resistant to medical therapy. Shock with a high sodium gets 0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid first, whatever the sodium (KJIM). Torsades goes to pw_palpitations.

Torsades: the palpitations pathway (pw_palpitations) takes it from here: magnesium sulfate 2 g IV whatever the serum magnesium, repeated if runs persist, every QT-prolonging drug stopped, potassium to 4.5 to 5, and an immediate shock if a run does not stop. The low magnesium and potassium are then replaced as in this pathway.

nodes.summary: Mild, symptom-free change: SfE says a calcium under 3.0 mmol/L is often asymptomatic and does not usually need urgent correction, so the PTH and cause are worked up (high PTH for hyperparathyroidism, low for malignancy or a rarer cause). A calcium above 1.9 mmol/L without symptoms is treated with oral calcium and its cause (vitamin D deficiency, low magnesium, recent neck surgery). An asymptomatic low magnesium is replaced by mouth (StatPearls). If every value is normal on repeat, there is no electrolyte emergency and the symptoms need another explanation.

nodes.ask: High potassium with ECG changes of hyperkalemia. First drug?
options: IV calcium gluconate now, repeated if the ECG has not improved
Insulin with glucose first; IV calcium if the QRS widens further
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g by mouth, then a repeat ECG
IV sodium bicarbonate as the first and main treatment
nodes.chainStep: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV (US consensus; UK: an equivalent 6.8 mmol), repeated if the ECG has not improved in 5 to 10 minutes; continuous cardiac monitoring; then shift and remove potassium
nodes.why: ECG changes mean the heart is at risk, so IV calcium comes first: it improves the ECG within about 3 minutes but does not lower the potassium, lasts only 30 to 60 minutes, and is repeated if there is no effect in 5 to 10 minutes. Calcium gluconate is preferred because calcium chloride can cause tissue necrosis if it extravasates. Insulin with glucose and albuterol follow at once to shift potassium into cells. Bicarbonate is not routine, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not recommended in the acute setting.

orders.dose: US consensus: calcium gluconate 1 g IV, repeated as needed; UK: an equivalent 6.8 mmol, the calcium in 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride (10 mL of 10% gluconate holds 2.26 mmol, so gluconate often needs sequential 10 mL doses); repeat if no effect in 5 to 10 minutes; gluconate no faster than 2 mL of 10% a minute (UKKA; FDA 200 mg a minute); JACEP may prefer chloride in the hemodynamically unstable patient
orders.note: Gluconate is preferred peripherally, since chloride causes tissue necrosis if it extravasates. The US and UK first doses differ about threefold. Same orders as the palpitations pathway.

IV calcium chloride; 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose; sodium bicarbonate suggested (UKKA)

nodes.ask: High potassium on the laboratory sample, ECG normal. Next?
options: Confirm it on a blood gas now, or a fresh free-flowing sample
IV calcium gluconate for the number, before a repeat
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate by mouth, then home
Sodium bicarbonate infusion while the repeat sample is running
nodes.chainStep: Repeat the potassium on a blood gas or a fresh sample from a large vein with gentle traction, analysed promptly; paired clotted and lithium heparin samples and a blood count if pseudohyperkalemia is suspected
nodes.why: Pseudohyperkalemia is common and treating a false value can harm, so a value that lacks a clear explanation (StatPearls) or does not fit the history (JACEP) is confirmed before aggressive treatment; a blood gas gives the potassium while the laboratory result is awaited (UKKA), so it is checked first and treatment starts as soon as it confirms. Long transit or storage, a difficult draw, hemolysis, a high platelet or white cell count, EDTA contamination or a sample from the arm with a potassium drip all raise the measured value. IV calcium is for ECG evidence of hyperkalemia, bicarbonate is not routine, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not recommended in the acute setting.

orders.dose: Paired clotted (serum) and lithium heparin (plasma) samples from a large vein with gentle traction, analysed promptly; a full blood count

outcomes.if: Normal on the blood gas or plasma sample; first sample hemolyzed or clotted
Confirmed 6.0 or more on blood gas or plasma; blood count normal, ECG still normal
Confirmed 5.5 to 5.9 on blood gas or plasma; ECG normal

nodes.summary: Pseudohyperkalemia or a sampling error: no potassium-lowering treatment, which could only cause harm. UKKA confirms it with paired clotted and lithium heparin samples (a serum value more than 0.4 mmol/L above the plasma) and a blood count for a high platelet or white cell count; JACEP adds that when blood cells are the cause, a repeat serum value stays falsely high.

nodes.ask: Potassium 6.0 or more on the gas or the laboratory. Next, to bring it down?
options: Insulin 10 units IV with glucose, plus nebulized albuterol
Nebulized albuterol alone, keeping the insulin in reserve for later
IV sodium bicarbonate, with no acidosis on the gas
IV furosemide 40 mg alone to bring it down
nodes.chainStep: Insulin 10 units IV with glucose (UK: 10 units soluble insulin in 25 g glucose; US review: 10 units regular insulin with 50 mL of 50% dextrose); nebulized albuterol 10 to 20 mg as an adjunct; glucose checks up to 12 hours; potassium at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours
nodes.why: Insulin shifts potassium into cells within about 15 minutes and its effect lasts hours; glucose goes with it, and the glucose is checked for up to 12 hours because hypoglycemia is the main risk. UKKA recommends insulin-glucose at 6.5 or more and suggests it at 6.0 to 6.4. Nebulized albuterol, 10 to 20 mg, is an adjunct and is not used alone in severe hyperkalemia. Bicarbonate is not routine and has a place in metabolic acidosis, and a loop diuretic is not recommended as the sole agent. Shifting is temporary, so potassium is rechecked and removed.

orders.dose: UK: 10 units soluble insulin in 25 g glucose IV; US review: 10 units regular insulin with 50 mL of 50% dextrose; if pre-treatment glucose is under 7.0 mmol/L, 10% glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 hours
Nebulized salbutamol (albuterol) 10 to 20 mg as an adjunct; not alone in severe hyperkalemia
Not routine; it can still be used with acidosis
Potassium at least at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours; blood glucose at intervals up to 12 hours after insulin-glucose

Not on dialysis, still 6.5 or more or oliguric; after the shift

nodes.ask: On hemodialysis with severe hyperkalemia, the shift given. Next?
options: Urgent hemodialysis with nephrology; repeat the shift meanwhile
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate enema as the main removal
Repeat insulin and albuterol, then discharge once it is under 6.0
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate instead of dialysis
nodes.chainStep: Urgent hemodialysis (nephrology; critical care if no renal service on site); repeat insulin with glucose and albuterol while it is arranged; IV calcium again for toxic ECG changes; continuous monitoring; potassium rechecked after dialysis for rebound
nodes.why: Hemodialysis removes potassium most effectively and is the definitive treatment in end-stage kidney disease, so a dialysis patient with severe hyperkalemia is dialyzed urgently, with standard medical treatment while it is arranged and IV calcium for toxic ECG changes even when dialysis is close. Insulin and albuterol only shift potassium, peak within 30 to 90 minutes and last up to 4 to 6 hours, so discharge after a shift alone invites the rebound, which can also follow dialysis. The US binder labels rule them out as emergency treatment because of their delayed onset, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not recommended acutely.

UKKA lists SZC as an option at 6.5 or more, although the US label says it is not emergency treatment. A second shift only redistributes potassium, so discharge on a lower number invites the rebound; sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not recommended acutely, and loop diuretics belong to a patient who passes urine and are not sole agents.

options: Stop culprit drugs and potassium; a binder if it stays high

nodes.chainStep: Stop potassium supplements; review and withhold culprit drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, heparin and others), withholding RAAS inhibitors in acute illness; low-potassium diet; a binder if it stays high; furosemide only if volume overloaded; potassium rechecked; community blood tests after discharge
nodes.why: Exogenous potassium is stopped at once, and every medicine that raises potassium is reviewed against the illness and kidney function: RAAS inhibitors are withheld during acute illness at any level of hyperkalemia, and their risk is weighed before they are restarted. Binders act over hours, not minutes (UKKA: calcium resonium over 4 hours, patiromer 4 to 7 hours, SZC about 1 hour; the US sodium polystyrene sulfonate label says hours to days), and the newer binders are preferred over sodium polystyrene sulfonate, which is not given with sorbitol because of intestinal necrosis. Loop diuretics are adjuncts for a volume-overloaded patient who passes urine, not sole agents. Every treated episode gets community potassium checks after discharge.

Potassium at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours and glucose for up to 12 hours after insulin. JACEP admits new-onset hyperkalemia and considers discharge only for chronic hyperkalemia whose cause is found and fixed, with stable vitals and follow-up within 24 to 48 hours.

nodes.ask: Low potassium with paralysis from a shift, no losses. Replacement?
options: Oral potassium chloride; IV in mannitol only for arrhythmia, swallow or breathing
IV potassium chloride in saline at 40 mEq an hour by central line, on a cardiac monitor
IV potassium chloride in 5% dextrose at 20 mEq an hour, on continuous ECG
Acetazolamide now, to end the attack and the paralysis
nodes.chainStep: Oral potassium chloride first; IV only for an arrhythmia, a failed swallow or respiratory muscle weakness, as 40 mEq/L in 5% mannitol at no more than 20 mEq/h, at most 200 mEq in 24 hours, on continuous ECG; potassium followed for 24 hours for rebound hyperkalemia; ECG and thyroid tests at a first attack
nodes.why: In periodic paralysis the potassium has shifted into cells and total body potassium is not depleted, so aggressive repletion can cause rebound hyperkalemia. Oral potassium chloride comes first; IV potassium is kept for arrhythmias, swallowing difficulty or respiratory muscle paralysis, and is given in mannitol rather than dextrose or saline, because carbohydrate and sodium can trigger paralysis, with continuous ECG monitoring. The potassium is followed for 24 hours, since it can keep rising as potassium leaves the cells. In thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, treatment of the hyperthyroidism is the mainstay; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors prevent familial attacks but may worsen the thyrotoxic form.

Thyroid function tests and an ECG

In thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, treatment of the hyperthyroidism is the mainstay.

nodes.ask: Potassium under 2.5, or low with ECG changes or paralysis. Replacement?
options: IV potassium chloride in saline by pump, on a monitor
Oral potassium chloride alone, 40 mEq now by mouth
Potassium chloride in 5% dextrose, run through an infusion pump
A 20 mEq potassium chloride IV push over 2 minutes
nodes.chainStep: IV potassium chloride, premixed in saline, by infusion pump: up to 10 mEq/h at up to 40 mEq/L when potassium is above 2.5; up to 40 mEq/h with continuous ECG monitoring and frequent levels, preferably by central line, when under 2.0 with ECG changes or paralysis; potassium every 2 to 4 hours; magnesium checked
nodes.why: Under 2.5 the oral label switches to IV potassium, and IV is preferred with arrhythmias, digoxin toxicity or ischemia. Concentrated potassium chloride must be diluted and given at a slow, controlled rate, in saline rather than dextrose because dextrose lowers potassium, and a central route is preferred whenever possible. Above 2.5 the rate stays at or under 10 mEq/h; up to 40 mEq/h is for a potassium under 2.0 with ECG changes or paralysis, with continuous cardiac monitoring, because rapid infusion can cause arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Peripheral infusions above 10 mmol/h cause pain and phlebitis.

options: Oral potassium chloride, 40 to 100 mEq a day in divided doses
IV potassium chloride 40 mEq over 1 hour through a hand vein
A high-potassium diet alone in place of a supplement
Oral potassium chloride, 100 mEq taken as one single dose today

nodes.why: Mild to moderate hypokalemia is usually treated by mouth, which carries less risk of rebound hyperkalemia. The label treats with 40 to 100 mEq a day, divided so that no single dose exceeds 40 mEq, and switches to IV only under 2.5. Extra dietary potassium is usually inadequate, because most food potassium comes with phosphate rather than chloride. A peripheral infusion faster than 10 mmol/h causes pain and phlebitis.

orders.dose: 40 to 100 mEq a day in divided doses, no more than 40 mEq per dose (FDA); StatPearls: 60 to 80 mmol a day over days to weeks

nodes.ask: Replacement under way. Which deficiency keeps potassium from correcting?
options: Low magnesium; check it and replace it
Low calcium; check it and replace it
Low phosphate; check it and replace it
Low sodium; check it and replace it
nodes.chainStep: Serum magnesium with the potassium; magnesium replaced if low; potassium rechecked every 2 to 4 hours
nodes.why: Low magnesium often coexists with low potassium (diarrhea, alcohol, diuretics, chemotherapy), increases urinary potassium loss and hinders replacement, so potassium alone may not correct until magnesium is replaced; the pair also raises the risk of torsades. The oral label likewise asks for attention to magnesium. Calcium, phosphate and sodium are worth measuring, but none of them is named as a block to potassium replacement.

orders.dose: Check it with the potassium and correct it if low; potassium replacement alone may be ineffective

nodes.summary: Hypokalemia: oral potassium chloride for 2.5 to 3.4 with a normal ECG; IV potassium chloride in saline for under 2.5, ECG changes, arrhythmia or paralysis, at up to 10 mEq/h above 2.5 and up to 40 mEq/h only for under 2.0 with ECG changes or paralysis on continuous monitoring; magnesium replaced; the cause treated (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, insulin, hyperaldosteronism); potassium every 2 to 4 hours. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis carries a high risk of rebound hyperkalemia during replacement.

Correct the sodium back to 135 mmol/L within 24 hours
0.9% saline, 1 L over an hour, to raise the sodium
nodes.chainStep: 3% saline: SfE 150 mL IV over 20 minutes, sodium checked while a second 150 mL runs, repeated twice or until a 5 mmol/L rise (US review: 100 mL boluses over 10 minutes as needed, for 4 to 6 mEq/L); then stop, keep the line open with minimal 0.9% saline and treat the cause; sodium at 6 and 12 hours, then daily
nodes.why: Severe symptoms (vomiting, seizures, cardiorespiratory arrest, reduced consciousness or coma) need hypertonic saline at once whatever the cause: the aim is a rise of about 5 mmol/L (4 to 6 in the US review), enough to reverse the danger from cerebral edema while limiting the risk of osmotic demyelination; management follows the symptoms, not the number. Urine osmolality and sodium define the cause after the emergency treatment, severe symptoms need immediate hypertonic saline rather than fluid restriction, and correcting to normal within a day breaks every 24-hour limit in the sources.

nodes.ask: After hypertonic saline, the sodium has risen past the 24-hour limit. Next?
options: Stop the hypertonic fluid; expert help with D5W and desmopressin
Continue the 3% saline; a fast rise is safe once symptoms settle
Restrict fluid to under 800 mL a day to hold the sodium steady
Tolvaptan 15 mg to steady the sodium overnight

nodes.why: Over-correction risks osmotic demyelination, and low potassium, alcohol, malnutrition and liver disease add to the risk. SfE stops hypertonic fluid once the rise passes 10 mmol/L in 24 hours or 18 in 48, and asks a clinician experienced in over-correction to consider hypotonic fluid with or without anti-diuresis; StatPearls uses 5% dextrose with desmopressin to bring the rise back within the limit. Fluid restriction and tolvaptan both push the sodium higher, and tolvaptan's own label warns that a rise over 12 mEq/L in 24 hours can cause osmotic demyelination.

nodes.ask: Low sodium, no severe symptoms now. Which tests define the cause?
options: Serum and urine osmolality, urine sodium, and a volume exam
Tolvaptan 15 mg today while the tests are running
CT head first, then the blood and urine tests if it is normal
Correct to 135 with 3% saline, then look for the cause
nodes.chainStep: Serum osmolality, glucose and lipids (to exclude pseudohyponatremia and a high glucose); urine osmolality and urine sodium; clinical volume status; TSH and cortisol; drug history (thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine and others)
nodes.why: Urine osmolality and urine sodium are central to the cause, read with the volume status: under 100 mOsm/kg points to primary polydipsia, low solute intake or inappropriate IV fluid; at 100 or more, a urine sodium under 30 points to a low effective volume and over 30 to SIADH, drugs, salt wasting, vomiting or adrenal insufficiency, while diuretics make the urine sodium unreliable. Serum osmolality, glucose and lipids exclude pseudohyponatremia, and hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency are excluded before SIADH is called. A head CT comes later, in the search for a central nervous system cause. Tolvaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia, and fast correction to normal breaks the 24-hour limit.

Once volume is restored a water diuresis can make the sodium rise unpredictably, so it is checked often against the 24-hour limit. With a diuretic on board the urine sodium cannot separate the causes, so SfE still considers every other cause. Fluid restriction is for euvolemic hyponatremia, tolvaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia, and hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms.

Hyponatremia with edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome): StatPearls treats the underlying condition, restricts salt and fluid, and gives loop diuretics. Tolvaptan is labeled for clinically significant hypervolemic hyponatremia, including heart failure, started only in hospital and limited to 30 days; its label says to avoid it in liver disease, including cirrhosis, so it is not used in cirrhosis.

Hyponatremia on a diuretic, not dry, urine sodium over 30: the diuretic makes the urine sodium unreliable, so SfE considers every other cause, SIADH included, and StatPearls turns to the fractional excretion of urea (over 55%) or uric acid (over 10%). Thiazides impair urinary dilution and are a common drug cause. Euvolemic hyponatremia is treated with fluid restriction under 1 L a day; severe symptoms still get 3% saline.

Isotonic saline may not correct SIADH and can make it worse, because the urine is more concentrated than the saline. If restriction fails, salt tablets with a loop diuretic or a vaptan come next, and tolvaptan is started and restarted only in hospital with close sodium monitoring. Demeclocycline and lithium are for when other therapies fail.

nodes.why: Hypernatremia is a water deficit: total body water times (sodium/140 minus 1), plus ongoing losses, replaced by mouth or tube where possible or with hypotonic fluid over 48 to 72 hours. When it has lasted more than 48 hours or its duration is unknown, the sodium falls no faster than 0.5 mmol/L an hour (12 a day), with checks every 2 to 4 hours, because rapid correction risks cerebral edema; a fall of 1 to 2 mmol/L an hour is reserved for acute hypernatremia from sodium loading within 48 hours. Isotonic saline is for shock or hypotension first, and diuretics belong to sodium overload, given with 5% dextrose.

Glucocorticoids are second line, for lymphoma, other granulomatous disease or vitamin D excess. Above 3.5 mmol/L the risk of arrhythmia and coma makes correction urgent.

Hypercalcemia with a high PTH: primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism. After IV saline, an IV bisphosphonate if more treatment is needed, and parathyroidectomy can be considered in an acute presentation with severe hypercalcemia and a poor response to other measures. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia can mimic it but is rarely severe or an emergency.

Hypercalcemia from lymphoma, granulomatous disease or vitamin D excess: glucocorticoids (SfE: prednisolone 40 mg daily, usually effective in 2 to 4 days) after IV saline, with an IV bisphosphonate if more treatment is needed.

Calcium normal after rehydration: the cause is still sought (a high PTH for hyperparathyroidism, a low PTH for malignancy or a rarer cause such as thiazides, lithium, vitamin D, immobilization or thyrotoxicosis), and drugs and supplements that raise calcium are reviewed.

calculators.title: Free water deficit
calculators.note: Total body water is 60% of weight in men and 50% in women and older men (StatPearls); KJIM deducts 5% in older adults, giving 45% in an older woman. In water-depleted patients KJIM uses 50% and 40% of lean weight. Add insensible and ongoing losses, and replace over 48 to 72 hours.

calculators.title: Oral potassium chloride, periodic paralysis
calculators.note: The repeat dose can follow every 30 minutes; no more than 200 mEq by mouth in 24 hours. Body stores are not depleted, so rebound hyperkalemia is the risk; some give 10 mEq an hour instead.

calculators.title: Calcitonin for hypercalcemia (label)

outputs.label: No response in 1 to 2 days: every 12 hours

calculators.note: SC or IM. If the response is still unsatisfactory after 2 more days, the maximum is 8 USP Units/kg every 6 hours.

calculators.title: Calcium gluconate infusion (label start)
calculators.note: Adults, after the bolus; titrated to serum calcium every 1 to 4 hours, starting at the low end in renal impairment. SfE instead dilutes 100 mL of 10% in 1 L and runs it at 50 to 100 mL/h.

calculators.title: 5% dextrose to re-lower the sodium
calculators.note: Should lower the sodium by about 2 mEq/L; continued until the goal is reached, with or without desmopressin 2 to 4 mcg IV or SC.

calculators.title: IV potassium phosphate (label)
calculators.note: Phosphorus, at most 45 mmol a dose, and only with potassium under 4. No faster than 6.8 mmol/h peripherally or 15 centrally. Low end with eGFR 30 to 59; consider an adjusted weight well above ideal.

calculators.title: Oral phosphate replacement (review)
calculators.note: Total for 24 hours, in 3 to 4 divided doses. IV instead when under 1 mg/dL with symptoms, or when oral replacement cannot be taken.

calculators.title: Refeeding: first days (NICE)
calculators.note: Extreme means, for example, BMI under 14 or negligible intake for more than 15 days, with continuous cardiac monitoring. Build up to full needs over 4 to 7 days. Supplements unless pre-feeding levels are high.
